intro: How Spanish people talk with their friends, and where not to use that language.
p.vale.consejo: It is used to accept something: «Vale, nos vemos a las ocho». It is very common in Spain.
p.venga.consejo: It is used to encourage or to close a chat: «¡Venga, hasta luego!».
p.qué va.consejo: It is colloquial and emphatic: «¿Caro? ¡Qué va!». Avoid it in formal situations.
p.ni idea.consejo: It is a short, colloquial way of saying «I don't know». With a boss, better «no lo sé».
p.me da igual.glosa: I don't mind, I don't care
p.me da igual.consejo: It works like «gustar»: «a mí me da igual». It can sound curt, so mind your tone.
p.mola.consejo: It comes from «molar», which works like «gustar»: «me mola esta canción». It is very colloquial.
p.guay.consejo: It is written «guay» and sounds «gwai». It is colloquial and fits almost anything good.
p.qué rollo.consejo: It is colloquial. The initial r of «rollo» sounds strong: «RRO-yo».
p.hecho polvo.consejo: Literally it is «made into dust». For a woman: «hecha polvo». It is colloquial.
p.flipar.glosa: to be amazed, to freak out
p.flipar.consejo: It is a colloquial verb: «flipo con este paisaje». It is regular, like «hablar».
p.un montón.consejo: It is used as an adverb: «me gusta un montón». It is colloquial; in formal speech, «mucho».
p.pasta.consejo: Besides the Italian food, in Spain «pasta» is money: «no tengo pasta».
p.curro.consejo: It comes from «currar», to work. It is colloquial: with your bosses, better «trabajo».
p.finde.consejo: It is the short form of «fin de semana». It is colloquial and very common.
b1.texto:
- To agree or close: **vale**, **venga**, **hecho**.
- To deny: **qué va**, **para nada**, **ni hablar**.
- Not to know or care: **ni idea**, **yo qué sé**, **me da igual**.
- To react: **¡Anda!**, **¡No me digas!**, **¡Qué fuerte!**, **¡Qué rollo!**, **¡Qué guay!**
- To address someone: **tío**, **tía**; and **hombre** or **mujer** for emphasis.
- To say «a lot»: **un montón**, **mogollón**.

Colloquial verbs: **currar** (to work), **molar** (to like), **flipar** (to be amazed), **pillar** (to catch, to get).

Colloquial nouns: **la pasta** (money), **el curro** (the job).

Spanish also shortens words: **el finde**, **la peli**, **el profe**, **el boli**, **el cole**.

All of this is for friends and family. In an interview, an email or with a stranger, use the neutral word.
b2.f0.texto: How is it going in the new job?
b2.f4.texto: Is so much work worth it for you?
b2.f6.texto: Shall we meet at the weekend?
b2.f7.texto: I will let you know on Friday.
b4.texto:
Every colloquial word has a neutral one. Choose according to whom you are talking to.

- **currar** → trabajar
- **la pasta** → el dinero
- **molar** → gustar
- **flipar** → sorprenderse mucho
- **un montón** → mucho
- **el finde** → el fin de semana
- **estar hecho polvo** → estar muy cansado

**Molar** works like **gustar**: **me mola** this song, **nos molan** Sundays.

**Register.** With friends and family, colloquial speech sounds natural. With a boss, in an email or in an interview, it sounds too informal.
b4.e0.texto: My brother works on Saturdays for the money.
b4.e2.texto: Last weekend I was amazed by the landscape.
b5.f0.texto: Saturday dawns with a clear sky over the rooftops.
b5.f1.texto: In the square, the bars put their tables out in the sun.
b5.f2.texto: A group of friends laughs loudly beside the fountain.
b5.f3.texto: Their quick voices blend with the clatter of the cups.
b5.f4.texto: A short-haired girl tells about her week with her hands.
b5.f5.texto: Her friends listen with eyes wide open.
b5.f6.texto: Every story ends in a burst of laughter that shakes the chairs.
b5.f7.texto: The waiter passes quickly with a tray full of coffees.
b5.f8.texto: The tower bells strike twelve over the square.
b5.f9.texto: Everyone gets up slowly and says goodbye with a long hug.
b6.o0.refuerzo: That is it: it means you have no preference.
b6.o1.refuerzo: That is denying something, and nobody has claimed anything.
b6.o2.refuerzo: That says you do not know, not that you do not mind.
b6.pregunta: You are asked «¿Pizza o pasta?» and do not mind. What do you say?
b7.o2.refuerzo: «Quedar» is to arrange to meet or to remain.
b7.pregunta: Complete, colloquially: I really like this song.
b8.o0.refuerzo: «Molar» is to like or to be great.
b8.o1.refuerzo: That is it: «currar» is to work, and «el curro» is the job.
b9.o2.refuerzo: That is it: «pasta» is money in slang.
b9.pregunta: Complete with the slang word for «dinero».
b11.o0.refuerzo: That is it: it is too informal for that moment.
b11.o1.refuerzo: That is exactly where you hear it.
b11.pregunta: Where would «¡Qué va, tío!» sound wrong?
b12.pregunta: Write the colloquial form of «el fin de semana».
p.pagan.consejo: From «pagar», to pay. The «g» before «a» is hard. The «-an» ending is for «ellos».
p.curra.consejo: Colloquial for «trabaja», from «currar». The «rr» in the middle is strong.
p.flipé.consejo: Colloquial for being very amazed. The accent on the «é» marks the past tense for «yo».
p.bares.consejo: Plural of «bar». In Spain bars often put tables outside. The stress falls on «BA».
p.carcajada.consejo: A loud, sudden laugh. The «j» sounds like a strong «h», so the stress falls on «HA».
p.currar.consejo: A colloquial infinitive for «trabajar». Use it with friends, not with your boss.
